planting.note: Plant divisions in early fall in rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; black false hellebore tolerates full sun only where soil never dries out, and is slow to reach flowering size.

directions: Veratrum nigrum is a rare and stately Eurasian woodland perennial producing large, parallel-veined, deeply pleated foliage spirally arranged on strong erect stems, topped from June to September by narrow, branched panicles 18-24 inches long of small, star-shaped, dark purple-to-blackish flowers quite unlike the greenish-yellow or white blooms of its American relatives. It makes a dramatic, long-lived anchor for a mixed woodland border, pairing well with ornamental grasses and lighter-colored companions. All parts of this plant, including the rhizome, are poisonous if ingested; handle with gloves and keep away from children, pets, and livestock.

planting.note: Plant divisions in early fall into deep, fertile, moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil in partial shade; plants left undisturbed for years form permanent, long-lived colonies.

directions: Veratrum album is a tall European and west Asian woodland perennial with stout, pleated, alternate leaves on simple stems, bearing branched spikes of white flowers marked with green from July into August. It succeeds in full sun only where soil stays constantly moist, but performs most reliably in cool, semi-shaded sites. All parts of the plant are poisonous, and the emerging leaves have caused serious accidental poisonings when mistaken for wild garlic or ramps; site it away from areas where edible greens are foraged and keep children, pets, and livestock away.

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring in cool, humus-rich, evenly moist woodland soil in shade; Ranzania is slow to establish and resents root disturbance, so choose a permanent site.

directions: Ranzania japonica is a monotypic Japanese genus in the barberry family related to Podophyllum, native to mountain woodlands of Honshu. Fleshy stems rise from a creeping rhizome, each bearing a pair of trifoliate compound leaves between which nodding, cup-shaped, mauve-to-lilac flowers appear in spring before the foliage fully expands. It remains rare and highly sought by woodland-plant collectors, forming slowly expanding colonies in a cool, sheltered peat or woodland bed once established.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in cool, moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in shade; this coastal relative of vanilla leaf spreads by rhizome into a dense colony once established in consistently moist conditions.

directions: Achlys californica is native to coastal conifer forests of California and southern Oregon and closely resembles its more widespread relative A. triphylla, forming the same deciduous, fan-shaped, three-lobed leaf carpet topped by slender petal-less white flower spikes in late spring, but is distinguished by its central leaflet bearing six to twelve teeth rather than the three or four typical of A. triphylla. As with its relative, the dried foliage releases a sweet vanilla fragrance. It makes an elegant textural groundcover under redwoods and other acid-loving shade plants, needing consistently cool, moist soil and intolerant of hot, dry summers.

planting.note: Transplant rooted runners in early spring into cool, acidic, humus-rich soil with sharp drainage, ideally on a shaded slope or among rocks where water never stands.

directions: This holly-leaved variety of the Japanese woodland native Shortia soldanelloides is distinguished from the typical form by its smaller, sharply spine-toothed leaves resembling miniature holly foliage, which take on bronze and red winter tones. In early spring, wiry stems lift the same dainty, nodding, deeply fringed pink-to-white bells above the foliage mat. It shares the species' need for cool, consistently moist summers and resents heavy clay or soil that dries out, making it a choice subject for a shaded rock garden or peat bed.
